## Q1
The number of positive integers not exceeding 100 that are either odd or the square of an integer is \_\_\_\_.

## Q1 - Options
(A) 63
(B) 59
(C) 55
(D) 50

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q1

There are 50 odd integers through 100. Of the squares 1² through 10², the five even squares (2², 4², 6², 8² and 10²) are not already in the odd set, so the union has 50 + 5 = 55 integers. Counting all ten squares again would double-count the five odd squares.

## Q2
How many ways are there to pack six copies of the same book into four identical boxes, where a box can contain as many as six books?

## Q2 - Options
(A) 4
(B) 6
(C) 7
(D) 9

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q2

Because both books and boxes are identical, each arrangement is a partition of 6 into at most four positive parts. The nine partitions are 6; 5+1; 4+2; 4+1+1; 3+3; 3+2+1; 3+1+1+1; 2+2+2; and 2+2+1+1.

## Q3
Which of the following pairs of propositions are not logically equivalent?

## Q3 - Options
(A) ((p → r) ∧ (q → r)) and ((p ∨ q) → r)
(B) p ↔ q and (¬p ↔ ¬q)
(C) ((p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q)) and p ↔ q
(D) ((p ∧ q) → r) and ((p → r) ∧ (q → r))

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Propositional & Predicate Logic
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q3

The first expression in option D requires r only when both p and q are true. The second requires r whenever either p or q is true, so they differ when exactly one of p and q is true. The other pairs are standard equivalent rewritings.

## Q4
Consider the linear programming problem:

Maximise Z = 2x₁ + 3x₂<br>
Subject to 2x₁ + x₂ ≤ 4; x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 5; x₁, x₂ ≥ 0.

The optimum value of the LP is

## Q4 - Options
(A) 23
(B) 9.5
(C) 13
(D) 8

## Q4 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Linear Programming & Transportation Problem
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q4

A linear-programming optimum occurs at a feasible corner. The two binding constraints give x₁ = 1 and x₂ = 2, so Z = 2(1) + 3(2) = 8. The other corners give smaller values.

## Q5
Consider a machine with byte-addressable main memory of 2¹⁶ bytes and block size 8 bytes. A direct-mapped cache has 32 lines. How many bits are in the tag, line, and word fields of a main-memory address?

## Q5 - Options
(A) 8, 5, 3
(B) 8, 6, 2
(C) 7, 5, 4
(D) 7, 6, 3

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Memory Hierarchy, Cache & Access Time
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q5

A 2¹⁶-byte memory uses 16 address bits. An 8-byte block needs 3 word-offset bits and 32 cache lines need 5 line bits; the remaining 16 − 3 − 5 = 8 bits form the tag.

## Q6
The following basic-computer program is stored in memory. What is the accumulator content after execution?

210 CLA<br>
211 ADD 217<br>
212 INC<br>
213 STA 217<br>
214 LDA 218<br>
215 CMA<br>
216 AND 217<br>
217 1234H<br>
218 9CE2H

## Q6 - Options
(A) 1002H
(B) 2011H
(C) 2022H
(D) 0215H

## Q6 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** COA: Arithmetic, Microprogramming, I/O & Multiprocessors
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q6

CLA clears AC; ADD 217 and INC produce 1235H, which STA stores at 217. LDA 218 loads 9CE2H, CMA gives 631DH, and 631DH AND 1235H equals 0215H.

## Q7
A non-pipeline system takes 50 ns per task. The same task uses a six-segment pipeline with a 10 ns clock. Determine the approximate speedup for 500 tasks.

## Q7 - Options
(A) 6
(B) 4.95
(C) 5.7
(D) 5.5

## Q7 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Pipelining & Amdahl's Law
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q7

Non-pipelined time is 500 × 50 = 25,000 ns. Pipeline time is (6 + 500 − 1) × 10 = 5,050 ns, including fill time. The speedup is 25,000/5,050 ≈ 4.95. A speedup of 6 ignores pipeline fill and drain overhead.

## Q8
What is the radix of the numbers if the solution to x² − 10x + 26 = 0 is x = 4 and x = 7?

## Q8 - Options
(A) 8
(B) 9
(C) 10
(D) 11

## Q8 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Combinational/Sequential Circuits, Flip-Flops & Number Systems
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q8

By Vieta’s rule, the sum of the roots is the value represented by 10 in that radix. Since 4 + 7 = 11 in decimal, 10 in the unknown base is 11, so the base is 11.

## Q9
Consider the pseudocode with integers a and b, where a &gt; 1 and a &lt; b:

int x = 0; int p = 1;<br>
while (p &lt; b) { p = p \* a; x = x + 1; }

When the loop terminates, what is x in terms of a and b?

## Q9 - Options
(A) ⌊logₐ b⌋
(B) ⌈logₐ b⌉
(C) logₐ b
(D) aᵇ

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q9

After x iterations, p = aˣ. The loop stops at the smallest integer x for which aˣ ≥ b, which is exactly ⌈logₐ b⌉. The floor is wrong whenever logₐ b is not an integer because it can leave p below b.

## Q11
A compiler uses 1-byte chars, 2-byte shorts, 4-byte ints, and 8-byte doubles. Every primitive must begin at an address that is a multiple of its size; fields cannot be reordered. How much space is consumed by an array A[10] of this structure?

struct { short s; char c; short t; char d; double r; int i; }

## Q11 - Options
(A) 150 bytes
(B) 320 bytes
(C) 240 bytes
(D) 200 bytes

## Q11 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q11

The layout is s at bytes 0–1, c at 2, padding at 3, t at 4–5, d at 6, then one byte of padding before double r at 8–15 and int i at 16–19. The structure is rounded to 24 bytes for 8-byte alignment, so ten elements occupy 240 bytes.

## Q12
Consider the recursive Java function:

public static float f(long m, long n) { float result = (float)m / (float)n;<br>
if (m &lt; 0 \|\| n &lt; 0) return 0.0f;<br>
else result -= f(m + 2, n \* 3);<br>
return result;<br>
}

Which real value best approximates f(1, 3)?

## Q12 - Options
(A) 0.2
(B) 0.4
(C) 0.6
(D) 0.8

## Q12 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q12

The recurrence alternates terms: 1/3 − 3/9 + 5/27 − 7/81 + …, stopping once m becomes negative in the recursive call chain. The partial sums settle near 0.2, whereas the larger choices ignore the alternating subtraction.

## Q14
For S = (U, V, W, X, Y, Z), the functional dependencies are {U → V, VW → X, Y → W, X → U}. Which listed sets are candidate keys?

## Q14 - Options
(A) UY, VY
(B) UY, VY, XY
(C) UYZ, VYZ, VWZ
(D) UYZ, VYZ, XYZ

## Q14 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Normalization & Functional Dependencies
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q14

Z never appears on the right-hand side, so every key must contain Z. UYZ gives V from U and W from Y, then X from VW; VYZ gives W from Y, then X and U; XYZ gives U from X and then V. Each is minimal, yielding option D.

## Q15
A machine has 3 page frames and the reference stream A, B, C, D, A, B, E, A, B, C, D, E, B, A, B. If P and Q are the page faults under FIFO and LRU respectively, what is (P, Q)?

## Q15 - Options
(A) (11, 10)
(B) (12, 11)
(C) (10, 11)
(D) (11, 12)

## Q15 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Memory Management, Page Replacement & Thrashing
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q15

Simulating FIFO replaces the oldest loaded page and produces 11 faults. Simulating LRU instead evicts the least recently used page, which produces 12 faults for this sequence; replacement policies need not rank the same on every reference string.

## Q16
A disk has 60 cylinders. Requests are 10, 22, 20, 2, 40, 6, 38; the head starts at 20. Movement by one cylinder takes 2 ms. Under SSTF, what is the total service time?

## Q16 - Options
(A) 240 milliseconds
(B) 96 milliseconds
(C) 120 milliseconds
(D) 112 milliseconds

## Q16 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Disk Scheduling, File Systems & RAID
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q16

SSTF serves 20, 22, 10, 6, 2, 38, 40, always choosing the nearest pending cylinder. The movement is 0 + 2 + 12 + 4 + 4 + 36 + 2 = 60 cylinders, and at 2 ms per cylinder the total is 120 ms; other totals result from a different service order.

## Q17
A Linux filesystem has 2 KB blocks and 32-bit disk addresses. An i-node has 12 direct pointers, one single-indirect pointer, and one double-indirect pointer. Approximately what is the largest representable file?

## Q17 - Options
(A) 513 Kbytes
(B) 513 Mbytes
(C) 537 Mbytes
(D) 537 Kbytes

## Q17 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Disk Scheduling, File Systems & RAID
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q17

A 2 KB indirect block contains 2,048/4 = 512 addresses. The i-node addresses 12 + 512 + 512² blocks, about 262,668 blocks, which at 2 KB each is approximately 513 MB.

## Q18
In a single-level page-table system with the page table in memory, TLB hit rate is 80%. TLB search takes 15 ns and a main-memory access takes 150 ns. What is the effective memory access time?

## Q18 - Options
(A) 185
(B) 195
(C) 205
(D) 175

## Q18 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Memory Management, Page Replacement & Thrashing
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q18

On a TLB hit, time is 15 + 150 = 165 ns. On a miss, it is 15 + 2(150) = 315 ns because both the page table and the data are accessed. The weighted average is 0.8(165) + 0.2(315) = 195 ns; treating every reference as a hit would wrongly give 165 ns.

## Q21
A company can use languages L₁ and L₂; an application needs three times as many LOC in L₂ as in L₁. The project has 10 years of maintenance. For what LOC in L₁ are the total development-plus-maintenance costs equal?

| Parameter | L₁ | L₂ |
|---|---|---|
| Man-years for development | LOC/1000 | LOC/1000 |
| Development cost | Rs. 70,000 | Rs. 90,000 |
| Maintenance cost per year | Rs. 1,00,000 | Rs. 40,000 |

## Q21 - Options
(A) 2000
(B) 6000
(C) 3000
(D) 5000

## Q21 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** COCOMO, Project Management & Risk
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q21

For x lines of L₁, development costs are 70x and 270x rupees for L₁ and L₂ respectively, since the rates are per 1,000 LOC and L₂ needs 3x lines. Ten-year maintenance costs are Rs. 10,00,000 and Rs. 4,00,000; equating totals gives 70x + 10,00,000 = 270x + 4,00,000, hence x = 3,000 LOC.

## Q22
A software project is estimated at 864 function points. A six-person team has one requirements gatherer (Rs. 50,000/month), one designer (Rs. 70,000/month), two programmers (Rs. 60,000/month each), and two testers (Rs. 60,000/month each). Team productivity is 12 FP per person-month. What is the projected cost?

## Q22 - Options
(A) Rs. 33,20,000
(B) Rs. 43,20,000
(C) Rs. 33,10,000
(D) Rs. 22,10,000

## Q22 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** COCOMO, Project Management & Risk
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q22

The effort is 864/12 = 72 person-months, or 72/6 = 12 calendar months for six people. Monthly payroll is 50,000 + 70,000 + 2(60,000) + 2(60,000) = Rs. 3,60,000, so the project cost is 12 × 3,60,000 = Rs. 43,20,000; it is not based on treating 864 as calendar months.

## Q23
A complete n-ary tree has either n children or no children at each node. If it has I = 10 internal nodes and L = 41 leaves, what is n?

## Q23 - Options
(A) 3
(B) 4
(C) 5
(D) 6

## Q23 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Graph Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q23

For a full n-ary tree, L = (n − 1)I + 1 because each internal node contributes n outgoing edges. Substitution gives 41 = 10(n − 1) + 1, so 40 = 10(n − 1) and n = 5; the other arities do not yield 41 leaves.

## Q24
In a binary max heap containing n numbers, the smallest element can be found in what time?

## Q24 - Options
(A) O(n)
(B) O(log₂ n)
(C) O(1)
(D) O(log log n)

## Q24 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q24

A max heap only guarantees that the largest element is at the root. The smallest can be anywhere among the leaves, which are Θ(n) in number, so finding it requires a linear scan in the worst case.

## Q25
Algorithm A takes log₂(n) microseconds and algorithm B takes √n microseconds. What are the largest problem sizes they can solve in one second?

## Q25 - Options
(A) 2²⁰ and 10⁸
(B) 2¹⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰ and 10¹²
(C) 2²⁰ and 6 × 10⁹
(D) 2¹⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰ and 6 × 10¹¹

## Q25 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q25

One second is 10⁶ microseconds. For algorithm A, log₂ n = 10⁶ gives n = 2¹⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰; for algorithm B, √n = 10⁶ gives n = 10¹². Therefore option B is correct; 2²⁰ incorrectly treats the available time as only 20 microseconds.

## Q26
Let G be a directed graph on vertices 1 through 100. There is an edge i → j exactly when j = i + 1 or j = 3i. What is the minimum number of edges in a path from 1 to 100?

## Q26 - Options
(A) 23
(B) 99
(C) 4
(D) 7

## Q26 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** BFS, DFS & Graph Algorithms
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q26

Breadth-first search gives the seven-edge path 1 → 3 → 9 → 10 → 11 → 33 → 99 → 100. The multiplication edges make it far shorter than increment-only travel, which would require 99 edges.

## Q27
Consider L = L₁ ∩ L₂, where L₁ = {0ᵐ1ᵐ20ⁿ1ⁿ \| m, n ≥ 0} and L₂ = {0ᵐ1ⁿ2ᵏ \| m, n, k ≥ 0}. Then L is

## Q27 - Options

(B) Regular
(C) Context-free but not regular
(D) Not recursive

## Q27 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** CFL, PDA, Pumping Lemma & Closure Properties
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q27

For a string to be in both languages, the portion after 2 in L₁ must be empty and the number of 1s before 2 must equal the number of 0s. Thus L reduces to {0ᵐ1ᵐ2 \| m ≥ 0}, which is context-free but not regular.

## Q28
Let L₁ and L₂ over Σ = {a, b} be represented by (a\* + b)\* and (a + b)\* respectively. Which statement is true?

## Q28 - Options
(A) L₁ ⊂ L₂
(B) L₂ ⊂ L₁
(C) L₁ = L₂
(D) L₁ ∩ L₂ = ∅

## Q28 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Finite Automata, Regular Languages & DFA Minimization
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q28

The inner expression a\* + b can generate either any run of a characters or a single b. Repeating it with the outer star generates every string over {a, b}, exactly as (a + b)\* does. Therefore L₁ = L₂; neither language excludes a mixed a/b string.

## Q29
Which statement is true?

## Q29 - Options
(A) The union of two context-free languages is context-free.
(B) The intersection of two context-free languages is context-free.
(C) The complement of a context-free language is context-free.
(D) Every context-free language can be accepted by a deterministic pushdown automaton.

## Q29 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** CFL, PDA, Pumping Lemma & Closure Properties
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q29

Context-free languages are closed under union. They are not closed under intersection or complement, and deterministic PDAs recognise only the smaller class of deterministic context-free languages.

## Q31
A code has valid words 0000000000, 0000011111, 1111100000, and 1111111111. If the received word is 0000000111, which word was sent?

## Q31 - Options
(A) 0000011111
(B) 0000000000
(C) 1111100000
(D) 1111111111

## Q31 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Hamming Code, Error Detection & Bit Stuffing
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q31

Decode by minimum Hamming distance. The received word differs from 0000011111 in two positions but from 0000000000 in three positions; the two words beginning with 11111 are farther away.

## Q32
Using RSA with p = 3, q = 11, and d = 7, find e and encrypt 19.

## Q32 - Options
(A) 20, 19
(B) 33, 11
(C) 3, 28
(D) 77, 28

## Q32 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Network Security & Cryptography
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q32

Here φ(n) = (3 − 1)(11 − 1) = 20. Since 7e ≡ 1 (mod 20), e = 3; with n = 33, encryption gives 19³ mod 33 = 28. Therefore option C is the only pair that has both the required inverse and ciphertext.

## Q34
The period of a signal is 100 ms. What is its frequency in kilohertz?

## Q34 - Options
(A) 10

(C) 10⁻⁷

## Q34 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Data Communication: Modulation, Multiplexing, Media & Topologies
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q34

The signal period is 100 ms, and frequency is its reciprocal. Because 100 ms = 0.1 seconds, its frequency is 1/0.1 = 10 Hz. Dividing by 1,000 converts this to 0.01 kHz = 10⁻² kHz; therefore the correct option is D.

## Q37
If f(x) means “x is my friend” and p(x) means “x is perfect”, translate: “Some of my friends are not perfect.”

## Q37 - Options
(A) ∀x (f(x) ∧ ¬p(x))
(B) ∃x (f(x) ∧ ¬p(x))

**Answer:** B

**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q37

“Some” requires an existential quantifier, and “not perfect” is ¬p(x). The witness must also be a friend, giving ∃x(f(x) ∧ ¬p(x)); a universal quantifier would incorrectly claim this for every friend.

## Q39
On A = {a,b,c,d,e,f,g}, R = {(a,a),(b,b),(c,d),(c,g),(d,g),(e,e),(f,f),(g,g)}. Which listed property is satisfied: reflexive, antisymmetric, symmetric?

For the premise ∀x(P(x) ∨ Q(x)), an argument tries to conclude (∀xP(x)) ∧ (∀xQ(x)) by instantiating P(c) ∨ Q(c) and then simplifying to P(c) and Q(c). Which assessment is correct?

(A) The argument is valid.

**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Propositional & Predicate Logic
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q40

From a disjunction P(c) ∨ Q(c), one cannot infer either disjunct by simplification. Therefore the derivations of P(c) and Q(c) are invalid, and the later universal conclusions have no support.

(A) (A) and (B) only
(B) (A) and (C) only

(D) (A), (B), and (C)

## Q41 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q41

A symbol table records identifiers and their attributes. Compilers consult it for storage allocation and type checking, and it also lets them recognise a repeated declaration so duplicate diagnostics are controlled. Thus all three listed uses apply.

## Q42
Which simplified expressions represent F(A,B,C,D) = Σ(0,1,2,3,6,12,13,14,15)?<br>
A. A′B′ + AB + A′C′D′<br>
B. A′B′ + AB + A′CD′<br>
C. A′B′ + AB + BC′D′<br>
D. A′B′ + AB + BCD′

## Q42 - Options
(A) (A) only
(B) (B) only
(C) (A) and (B) only
(D) (B) and (D) only

## Q42 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** K-Map, SOP & Boolean Laws
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q42

A′B′ covers minterms 0–3 and AB covers 12–15. Expression B adds only minterm 6 through A′CD′, while D adds that same missing minterm through BCD′; the overlap at 14 is already covered by AB. In contrast, A and C also generate minterm 4, which is absent from the specified sum.

**Answer:** A

**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q43

With balanced stages and a long stream, speed-up approaches k, but fill and drain overhead prevent a finite workload from reaching it exactly. Equal stage times are an ideal design goal, not a universal property.

A multiprocessor is a tightly coupled system managed by one OS and normally follows the MIMD model. Statement B instead describes a distributed system of separate computers.

## Q52
The running time of an algorithm is O(g(n)) if and only if

## Q52 - Options

**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q52

An algorithm is O(g(n)) when its worst-case running time has an asymptotic upper bound g(n). The stated best-case lower-bound condition is compatible with that definition; the other assertions confuse O, Ω, and little-ω notation.

## Q53

**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q53

Trees are bipartite, and bipartite is equivalent to 2-colourable. A bipartite graph forbids odd cycles, not even ones. Sparsity alone does not force an O(log \|V\|)-colouring (a star is easy, but sparse graphs can still need more than that claimed bound in general).

A fixed-size digest is produced from inputs of arbitrary size. Since the input space is much larger than the digest space, collisions—different inputs with the same digest—are possible.

Equivalence and proper inclusion for arbitrary context-free languages are undecidable. Equality with a regular language is also undecidable: choosing R = Σ\* would decide the undecidable universality problem for context-free grammars.

Ambiguity means that one terminal string can have two different parse trees. **Answer:** A

**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q80

Fermat’s little theorem gives n⁵ ≡ n (mod 5). Also n³ − n is the product of three consecutive integers, so it is divisible by 6; both statements are true.

A track holds 50 × 512 = 25,600 bytes, recorded as 25 K in the choices. A surface has 2,000 tracks, giving 2,000 × 25 K = 50,000 K. The 25,000 K option misses the factor from the number of tracks, while 50 K is only the sector-scale figure.

## Q95

**Answer:** D

**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q95

One track contains 50 sectors × 512 bytes = 25,600 bytes. ## Q97 - Options
(A) Both statements are true.
(B) Both statements are false.
(C) Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
(D) Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

## Q97 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q97

Statement I supplies the join predicate that relates an employee to a department before filtering by department name. Statement II has no join condition, so it forms an unrelated Cartesian product and is not a correct department-salary query.

## Q98
Which query returns employee ID and name for employees whose salary is greater than the salary of every employee in department 20, ordered by employee ID?<br>
A. uses SALARY &gt; (subquery) with ORDER BY.<br>
B. uses SALARY &gt; (subquery) without ORDER BY.<br>
C. uses SALARY &gt; ALL (subquery) with ORDER BY.

## Q98 - Options
(A) (A) and (B) only
(B) (A) and (C) only
(C) (B) only
(D) (C) only

## Q98 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q98

A scalar comparison with a subquery returning several salaries is not the required “greater than every” test and can be invalid. `> ALL (...)` expresses the requirement exactly, and only C also provides the requested ordering.

## Q99
Which SQL statement(s) can drop the SALARY column from EMPLOYEE?<br>
A. ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE DROP SALARY CASCADE;<br>
B. ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE DROP SALARY RESTRICT;<br>
C. ALTER EMPLOYEE DROP SALARY;

## Q99 - Options
(A) (A) and (B) only
(B) (A) and (C) only
(C) (B) and (C) only
(D) (A) only

## Q99 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q99

The supported form is `ALTER TABLE ... DROP ...`. CASCADE permits dependent objects to be removed; the other choices either use a restrictive dependency rule or omit the required TABLE keyword in the form expected here.

## Q100
Using the university table structures, the university wants to give every employee in the SCIENCE department a 20% salary rise. Which query is correct?<br>
A. UPDATE EMPLOYEE SET SALARY = SALARY \* 1.20 WHERE DEPTNO IN (SELECT DID FROM DEPARTMENT WHERE DNAME = 'SCIENCE');<br>
B. UPDATE TABLE EMPLOYEE SET SALARY = SALARY \* 1.20 WHERE DNAME = 'SCIENCE';<br>
C. ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE SET SALARY = SALARY \* 1.20 WHERE DEPTNO IN (SELECT DNAME FROM DEPARTMENT WHERE DNAME = 'SCIENCE');

## Q100 - Options
(A) (A) and (B) only
(B) (A) only
(C) (B) and (C) only
(D) (C) only

## Q100 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q100

A is valid: it updates EMPLOYEE rows whose department number belongs to the SCIENCE department. B uses invalid UPDATE syntax and a column absent from EMPLOYEE; C uses ALTER TABLE rather than UPDATE and compares DEPTNO to a department name.
